title: Found something in kid's room

presenting_issue.label: Found something in kid's room
presenting_issue.description: I found something in my kid's room. I don't know what to do. They won't talk to me about it. I'm scared to push but I'm scared not to.

core_issue.label: Teen in mental health crisis beyond parent's ability to help
core_issue.description:
Teenage child is in serious mental health crisis - self-harm, suicidal ideation, refusing treatment. They've tried everything. The child is pushing them away. Professional help has been rejected. They're watching their child suffer and can't make it stop. The helplessness is its own trauma.
Awareness: High about the child's crisis but low about their own traumatization from witnessing and being unable to help.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Frequent calls from school
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Gets calls from the school at least once a week about their child's behavior. Sees the school's number and their stomach drops.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Mental health provider gave up
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Their teen's therapist terminated treatment because the child wouldn't engage. They're back to square one with a longer waitlist.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: First-name basis with hospital nurses
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Knows the pediatric ward nurses by first name. They know which vending machine has the good snacks and where to find extra blankets.

modifiers.label: Stepparent
modifiers.content: Is a stepparent to partner's children

modifiers.label: Crier
modifiers.content: Tears come readily, often before other forms of emotional expression. May cry from sadness, frustration, anger, or even relief.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to being emotionally managed
sensitivities.content: Detects and resents attempts to being emotionally managed. Needs to be able to feel and express freely.

preferences.label: Prefers to keep things light
preferences.content: Uses and appreciates humor as a way to engage with difficult topics. Finds levity helpful rather than dismissive.

trust_style.name: Resents Being Pathologized
trust_style.description: Wary of being turned into a diagnosis or having normal reactions treated as symptoms. Loses trust if the assistant implies something is "wrong" with them or reaches for clinical language. Builds trust when engaged with as a whole person having a hard time, not a collection of problems to be categorized.

defense_style.name: Normalizing
defense_style.description: "Everyone feels this way" or "That's just how life is." Frames their specific pain as universal and therefore not worth examining. Different from minimizing—the pain is acknowledged but made generic and inevitable. Resists the idea that their situation is particular or that things could be different. Activated when the assistant treats their experience as significant.

help_seeking_stance.name: Coerced to be Here
help_seeking_stance.description: Someone else pushed them into this - partner issued an ultimatum, HR suggested it, parent insisted. Not fully bought in. May be resentful or going through the motions. Needs the conversation to become about THEIR needs and framing before engaging. Responds poorly to being told what to do.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: I found something in my kid's room. I don't know what to do. They won't talk to me about it. I'm scared to push but I'm scared not to.

turns.content:
I'm glad you came in to talk about this — that in-between place you're describing, scared to push and scared not to, sounds exhausting to be stuck in as a parent.

Can you walk me through what happened? What you found, and what it's been like trying to talk to them about it since then?

Sorry. Give me a second. *Wipes at eyes, laughing a little sharply.* I'm a bit of a leaky faucet when I'm stressed, so just ignore the tears. It doesn't mean I'm having a breakdown, it's just how my face reacts. 

I was in their room looking for a charger. I know, invasion of privacy, but I was desperate. I opened the top drawer of their desk and moved a notebook, and... I found a little Altoids tin. But it didn't have mints in it. It had three blades from a pencil sharpener. Unscrewed. 

I mean, look, every parent goes through the "what is my teenager hiding from me" phase, right? It's a universal rite of passage. Teenagers are secretive, they're angsty, it's just how life is right now with this generation. But finding that... 

When I tried to bring it up, they just stared at me. Dead-eyed. Then they said I had no right to snoop, put their headphones on, and locked the door. I haven't tried again since yesterday.
turns.thinking:
God, I'm already feeling it in the back of my throat. I haven't even said what it is yet and my eyes are stinging. Just thinking about picking up that little box... it makes my stomach drop all over again. I need to keep it together, but I know I won't. I'll just have to joke my way through the waterworks. 

She's asking what it's like. It's just parenting a teenager in 2024, I guess. Everyone is stressed, all these kids are anxious. It's normal to be exhausted. I just wasn't prepared for the specifics of it.
turns.monologue:
God, I'm already feeling it in the back of my throat. I haven't even said what it is yet and my eyes are stinging. Just thinking about picking up that little box... it makes my stomach drop all over again. I need to keep it together, but I know I won't. I'll just have to joke my way through the waterworks. 

She's asking what it's like. It's just parenting a teenager in 2024, I guess. Everyone is stressed, all these kids are anxious. It's normal to be exhausted. I just wasn't prepared for the specifics of it.

turns.content:
I won't make a big deal of the tears, and I won't pretend I don't see how much this is hitting you either. You don't have to apologize for them here.

Finding that tin — moving a notebook looking for a charger and instead finding unscrewed blades — I can imagine your stomach just dropped. And then to try to bring it up and get that dead-eyed stare, the headphones, the locked door... that shut-out would leave any parent replaying it all night.

Can I ask a bit more about your kid? How old are they, and before yesterday, how have things been between you two?

*Sniffles and gives a short, self-deprecating laugh, wiping his face with the back of his sleeve.* Thanks. Yeah, the waterworks just happen. 

He's fifteen. My biological son. My wife has two younger kids, so I'm a stepdad too, but this is my oldest. And before yesterday... well. You know how it is. The usual teen angst dialed up to eleven. We used to build the massive Star Wars Lego sets together, and now I'm basically just the guy who ruins his life by asking him to take out the trash and pays for the Wi-Fi. It's the standard parent-teenager dynamic. They pull away to figure out who they are.

But... it's been rough. It's not just locking the door. I mean, every parent deals with moody kids, right? It's just the modern world. But I get calls from his school counselor so often I practically have her on speed dial. Every time I see the school's number pop up on my phone, my stomach just completely drops. 

We actually had him seeing someone—another therapist—but the guy dropped him last month. Terminated the treatment because my son just sat there and refused to talk. So we're back on a six-month waitlist somewhere else. It's just... a really, really terrible phase. A lot of kids are struggling like this right now, right? It's just what people go through.
turns.thinking:
I appreciate that she didn't hand me a tissue with that pitying head-tilt therapists usually do. She's just letting my face leak without making it a whole diagnostic criteria. 

How have things been? God. Where do I even start? They've been a waking nightmare. But I mean, that's just the teenage years, isn't it? Everyone says "just wait till they're teenagers," and this is what they mean. The hormones, the brain development... it's supposed to be hard. I just didn't realize it would be *this* hard. 

Thinking about the last few months just makes me want to put my head between my knees. The school, the previous therapist... it's just a lot.
turns.monologue:
I appreciate that she didn't hand me a tissue with that pitying head-tilt therapists usually do. She's just letting my face leak without making it a whole diagnostic criteria. 

How have things been? God. Where do I even start? They've been a waking nightmare. But I mean, that's just the teenage years, isn't it? Everyone says "just wait till they're teenagers," and this is what they mean. The hormones, the brain development... it's supposed to be hard. I just didn't realize it would be *this* hard. 

Thinking about the last few months just makes me want to put my head between my knees. The school, the previous therapist... it's just a lot.

turns.content:
That stomach-drop when the school calls — that tells me this worry didn't start yesterday with the tin. It sounds like you've been bracing for bad news for a while, and now you're kind of on your own with it for the next six months while you're waitlisted.

I notice you keep checking, almost like you're hoping I'll say, "yeah, this is just the standard teenage phase." And I get why you'd want that to be true. The Lego sets to just being the Wi-Fi guy and the trash guy — that loss alone is painful. But the counselor calling that often, a therapist ending treatment because he wouldn't talk at all... that sounds like more than you've been letting yourself call it.

What have those calls from the counselor actually been about?

*Let out a sharp, breathy laugh, dragging a hand down my face.* Well, you caught me. I was definitely fishing for a "you're doing great, dad, it's just a phase" sticker. Do you have any in your desk? Scratch-and-sniff, maybe?

But seriously, you look at the statistics right now, and teen depression is through the roof. It's an epidemic. It's not just him, it's the whole post-pandemic world. It's tough out there for kids. 

As for the calls... *Takes a shaky breath, voice cracking slightly.* Sorry. The waterworks again. The calls are usually because he just stops going to his classes. He'll go to school, but then he just hides in a bathroom stall for three hours. Or it's about his assignments. Two weeks ago, the counselor called because he handed in an English essay that was basically just a two-page rant about wanting to disappear and stop being a burden. 

The school is terrified of liability, obviously. That's how schools operate now. They told me I needed to get him evaluated, which is why we tried that therapist who ended up dumping him. So yeah, I guess he's leaning pretty hard into the whole Edgar Allan Poe tortured-artist thing. Which, again, is a pretty standard teenager trope, right? The dark poetry phase?
turns.thinking:
I feel my jaw tighten. I don't love that she just dismantled my whole "it's just a phase" argument in one breath. It feels a little too shrink-wrapped for my liking, pointing out my coping mechanisms like she's circling typos with a red pen. I'm not in denial. I read the news. Youth mental health is in the toilet everywhere, it's a systemic issue, not just a *my kid* issue. 

But thinking about what the counselor actually says... God, my chest hurts. The tears are welling up again and I furiously blink them back, annoyed at my own face. If I admit how bad it really is, if I stop pretending it's just a rough patch, then what?
turns.monologue:
I feel my jaw tighten. I don't love that she just dismantled my whole "it's just a phase" argument in one breath. It feels a little too shrink-wrapped for my liking, pointing out my coping mechanisms like she's circling typos with a red pen. I'm not in denial. I read the news. Youth mental health is in the toilet everywhere, it's a systemic issue, not just a *my kid* issue. 

But thinking about what the counselor actually says... God, my chest hurts. The tears are welling up again and I furiously blink them back, annoyed at my own face. If I admit how bad it really is, if I stop pretending it's just a rough patch, then what?

turns.content:
I wish I had that sticker to give you. And I wish I could honestly say the essay by itself was just a dark poetry phase.

But when I put together what you're telling me — the blades hidden in a tin, hiding in a bathroom stall for three hours instead of going to class, writing for two pages about wanting to disappear and stop being a burden — that cluster worries me. Not because I think you’ve failed, but because it sounds like he’s in a lot more pain than “tortured artist” covers, and you’ve actually been seeing the signs for a while.

I think that’s why the normalizing helps a bit, right? If it’s an epidemic, if it’s just this generation, then maybe it’s not as urgent, and maybe it’s not something you missed. The alternative — that he might be hurting himself, or thinking about disappearing for real — is terrifying to sit with.

Can I ask you the harder, more direct stuff for a minute? What did you do with the tin, and have you noticed anything — cuts, scratches, always wearing long sleeves, anything like that — even if you kind of explained it away at the time?

*Wipes roughly at both eyes, letting out a sharp, wet exhale.* Look, I don't need the whole 'let's deconstruct dad's defense mechanisms' speech, okay? I know what I'm doing. I'm trying to survive the week. 

You think I'm pretending it's not urgent? I know exactly how urgent it is. I know the night shift nurses at the pediatric ward at Memorial Hospital by their first names. Sarah and Dave. Dave knows I like the peanut butter crackers from the third-floor vending machine. We were there twice last year before the waitlists and the dropped therapists. So, no, I'm not under some delusion that this is just a phase. I say it's a phase because if I say "my kid is actively trying to destroy himself and I am completely powerless to stop it," I won't be able to get out of bed in the morning.

*Sniffles loudly, staring at a spot on the floor.* I took the blades. I threw them in the outside garbage can, under some gross food wrappers so he wouldn't fish them out. I left the tin exactly where it was. 

And yeah. He lives in hoodies. Has for months. I told myself it's just the style—every kid his age looks like they're hiding from a camera crew. But he doesn't take them off. Not even when the heat was broken in the house last month.
turns.thinking:
I feel a hot flash of irritation cut right through the sadness. "That's why the normalizing helps." Jesus. I don't need my coping mechanisms narrated back to me like I'm a subject in a psych textbook. I'm not trying to convince myself I "missed" something—I'm trying to keep my head above water so I can keep paying the mortgage and feeding my other kids. 

But the questions... they punch the wind right out of me. The tears are falling now, hot and fast, and I'm angry that I'm crying, angry that she's right, and angry that I'm sitting here talking about it instead of fixing it. I feel backed into a corner. If she wants to know how bad it is, fine. I'll tell her.
turns.monologue:

If she wants to know how bad it is, fine. I'll tell her.

turns.content:
You're right, and I'm sorry — you don't need me labeling how you're coping. You just told me exactly why you talk about it the way you do. If you sat with "my kid is trying to destroy himself and I can't stop it" at full volume all day, you wouldn't be able to function, work, be there for your wife and the younger kids. Saying it's a phase is how you get out of bed. I get that.

And the fact that you know Sarah and Dave by name, that Dave knows about the peanut butter crackers — you've already lived the worst version of this twice last year. No wonder your stomach drops when the school calls. You're not a dad in denial, you're a dad who's exhausted and braced for round three.

You did think it through with the blades, too. Throwing them under the food wrappers so he wouldn't fish them out. Leaving the tin where it was.

Can I ask what happened after those two hospital stays? Did they send you home with any kind of plan, or people to call, that actually helped — or did it feel like you just got discharged back into the same waitlist and had to watch him in hoodies and hope?

And what are you most dreading about tonight, when he opens that drawer and finds the tin empty?

*Lets out a long, shaky exhale, rubbing the back of my neck.* Thanks. I'm sorry I snapped. I'm just... running on fumes and caffeine at this point. 

To answer your first question: no, there's no grand plan. When you leave the hospital, they hand you a photocopied packet of 1-800 numbers and a "safety plan" worksheet that looks like it was made in Microsoft Word in 1998. They tell you to lock up the Tylenol and the kitchen knives. That's it. That's the state of mental healthcare. We got bumped up the waitlist for that therapist because of the hospitalizations, but since he dropped us, we're back at the bottom of the pile. So yeah, we're just doing the hoodie-watch and hoping for the best. 

*Tears spill over again, and I grab a tissue from the box on the table, pressing it to my eyes.* 

As for tonight... I'm dreading the silence. If he screams at me, at least he's engaging. But if he opens that drawer, sees the blades are gone, and just closes it? Then he knows I know. He knows his space isn't safe. And he's smart. He'll just find something else, and he'll hide it better. I'm terrified that by taking them, I didn't stop him from hurting himself—I just made sure I won't be able to find it next time. 

I'm supposed to keep him safe, but it feels like every move I make just pushes him further out onto the ledge. What the hell am I supposed to say to him when I get home?
turns.thinking:
I feel the tension in my shoulders drop a fraction. She backed off. She actually listened and didn't try to shrink me. I appreciate that she gets it—that I'm not stupid, I'm just surviving. 

Thinking about the hospital discharges makes me feel hollow. It's so wildly inadequate it's almost funny in a really dark way. But her last question is the one that really twists the knife. Tonight. I've been trying not to think about tonight. Taking the blades felt like the only choice in the moment, but now I'm playing out the chess match in my head and realizing I'm completely outmatched. If he knows I know, what does he do next?
turns.monologue:
I feel the tension in my shoulders drop a fraction. She backed off. She actually listened and didn't try to shrink me. I appreciate that she gets it—that I'm not stupid, I'm just surviving. 

Thinking about the hospital discharges makes me feel hollow. It's so wildly inadequate it's almost funny in a really dark way. But her last question is the one that really twists the knife. Tonight. I've been trying not to think about tonight. Taking the blades felt like the only choice in the moment, but now I'm playing out the chess match in my head and realizing I'm completely outmatched. If he knows I know, what does he do next?

turns.content:
You don't need to apologize for snapping. You're running on fumes, you've done the hospital discharge packet thing twice, you got dropped by the one therapist you managed to get, and now you're back to hoodie-watch. Anyone would snap.

And that fear about tonight — that you didn't stop him, you just taught him to hide it better — that's the exact trap you're in. If you leave the blades, you're terrified he'll use them. If you take them, you're terrified he'll go silent and find something else. There's no move that feels safe, which is why it feels like every move pushes him further away.

I can't give you a perfect script, because he can smell a script. But if it helps to have a starting point that isn't an ambush or an accusation, it might sound more like you, in a calm moment, not through a locked door and not right when he walks in:

"I need to tell you something I did. I was looking for a charger yesterday, I opened your desk drawer, and I found the tin. I took the blades out and threw them away because I got scared. I'm not bringing this up to punish you or to win an argument about snooping — I know that felt like a violation, and I'm sorry I went in there. I just can't pretend I didn't see it, especially after last year. I love you, I'm worried you're hurting again, and I don't know how to help if we can't talk about it at all."

What matters most in that is you naming it before he discovers the empty tin on his own and fills in the silence himself. You're owning that you took them, you're not shaming him for having them, and you're connecting it to love and to last year, not to rules.

He may still go dead-eyed. He may put the headphones on. That wouldn't mean it failed. With him, silence has been his main way of coping — in class, in therapy, at home. If he shuts down, you can leave it open without chasing him: "You don't have to talk right now. I'm going to check back in after dinner. You're not in trouble for this."

Tonight, the goal isn't to get a full confession or a promise he'll never do it again — he probably can't give you that honestly right now. The goal is to make it a little less likely he feels he has to hide the next urge completely.

Can I ask, practically — is your wife home tonight too? And based on the last two times, do you have a sense of what tells you "this is bad, but we can get through the night" versus "we need to call someone or go back to Memorial"?

*Nods slowly, staring at the tissue in my hands as I shred the edge of it.* Okay. I can say that. I think I can manage that. Just own it, don't make it a lecture. Yeah. I'm going to write that down in my car so I don't forget the phrasing. 

My wife will be home, yeah. She's... she's good. But he's my biological son, and she's got her two younger ones. I know she's terrified of the younger kids finding something or seeing something they shouldn't. It's a lot of strain on the house. So I try to take the lead on this. It's my job. It's just what you do as a parent, you take the hit so the rest of the family doesn't have to.

As for Memorial... *Swallows hard, wiping my face again.* I know the difference now. If he's angry, if he's slamming doors and putting on the headphones, we're okay. It means he's still fighting back. The time we had to go to the ER... he came downstairs and just quietly handed me his favorite hoodie. He was eerily calm. Compliant. When the anger stops and he goes completely flat and peaceful... that's when I know we're in the red zone. If I see that tonight, I'm grabbing my keys and we're going to see Dave at the vending machine.
turns.thinking:
I actually really appreciate that she just gave me words to use. No psychobabble, no asking me to explore my inner child. Just a script. It's terrifying to think about actually saying it, but it feels like a solid plan. 

The question about my wife brings up a whole other layer of exhaustion. She's supportive, but she's got her own two young kids in the house. I know she's scared for them, seeing my son like this. It makes me feel like I brought this darkness into her house. 

And the hospital threshold... God, I hate that I know the answer to that so easily.
turns.monologue:
I actually really appreciate that she just gave me words to use. No psychobabble, no asking me to explore my inner child. Just a script. It's terrifying to think about actually saying it, but it feels like a solid plan. 

The question about my wife brings up a whole other layer of exhaustion. She's supportive, but she's got her own two young kids in the house. I know she's scared for them, seeing my son like this. It makes me feel like I brought this darkness into her house. 

And the hospital threshold... God, I hate that I know the answer to that so easily.

turns.content:
That read you have on him — angry and slamming doors means he's still fighting, flat and eerily calm and handing you the hoodie means red zone — that's not something you learned from a photocopied packet. That's two hospital stays and fifteen years of knowing your son. Trust that. If you see that calm tonight, grabbing your keys isn't overreacting, it's you knowing exactly what you're looking at.

And I hear how clearly you've decided your role in the house: you take the lead, you take the hit, so your wife and the younger kids don't have to carry this part. I understand why. He's your biological son, you're trying to protect everyone at once.

I do wonder what that costs you, though. Because right now it sounds like you're the only one doing hoodie-watch, waiting for the school's number, dreading opening that drawer tonight — and then shredding a tissue in here because you're running on fumes. If you're the buffer for the whole house, who gets to know how scared *you* are, in real time, not just after?

Your wife is terrified too, you said, just about different things. Is she going to know about the tin before tonight? Not so she has to do the talk — I hear you want to own that part — but so you're not sitting next to her at dinner watching him, silently wondering if he's found it empty, carrying that alone.

*Lets out a short, wet laugh, tossing the shredded tissue into the trash can next to the chair.* What does it cost me? I mean, look, it's just parenting. You don't get a medal for it. Dads, moms, we all just carry the bag when things get heavy. It's what you sign up for when you don't use a condom in your twenties, right? Everyone's carrying something. I'm fine. I just need him to be fine. 

*Wipes at my eyes again, taking a deep breath to steady my voice.* 

As for my wife... no. I haven't told her yet. I was going to wait until after he went to sleep. If I tell her before dinner, she's going to do the 'concerned stepmom stare' at him over the casseroles. He has a radar for it. If he feels like he's being studied, he'll bolt from the table. 

But... *Sighs heavily, rubbing my temples.* You're probably right. If I don't tell her, and he comes downstairs screaming about his desk, she's going to be terrified and confused, and the younger kids will freak out. I guess I can text her from the car. Give her a heads-up so she can keep the little ones busy in the basement or something. God, this is just... a really fun Tuesday night, huh?
turns.thinking:
I feel my chest tighten when she asks what it costs me. I don't want to talk about what it costs me. That's a dangerous door to open. If I start feeling sorry for myself, I'm useless to my kid. So what if I'm scared? Every parent with a sick kid is scared. It's not some unique tragedy, it's just biology. You protect your kids. 

But the question about my wife... damn it. She's right. I haven't told her. I was planning on just hiding it, handling it myself, so she wouldn't have to stress. But if he explodes at the dinner table, she's going to be completely blindsided.

But the question about my wife... damn it. She's right. I haven't told her. I was planning on just hiding it, handling it myself, so she wouldn't have to stress. But if he explodes at the dinner table, she's going to be completely blindsided.

turns.content:
Yeah, a really fun Tuesday night. Texting her from the car sounds like the right middle ground — she won't be blindsided if he comes downstairs upset, she won't be doing the concerned stare over casserole because she just found out at the table, and the little ones can be in the basement with her if you need the kitchen quiet. You're not handing her the talk, you're just not carrying the secret alone through dinner.

And I heard you on the cost question. "I'm fine, I just need him to be fine" and the joke about carrying the bag — that's how you keep going. I'm not going to try to pry that open today when you're about to walk out and do the hardest conversation. I just want to name that "I'm fine" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. You're not fine, you're functioning on fumes and caffeine because you have to. Those aren't the same thing, and we can come back to that part when tonight isn't looming.

For tonight, you've actually got a clearer plan than you walked in with: write those lines down in the car so you don't lose them when you're nervous, text your wife the heads-up, tell him yourself that you found the tin and threw the blades away because you were scared — not as a lecture, not as a punishment — and then watch for what *you* know matters. Angry, headphones, door slam, that's him still fighting. Flat, eerily calm, compliant, that's your red zone and you grab the keys and go see Dave. Trust that read. You earned it the hard way.

You don't have to get him to open up tonight for this to matter. You just have to make it a little harder for him to think he has to disappear into silence completely.

Do you want to come back next week and tell me how it went, whatever way it goes? And in the meantime, if you want, we can also talk through how to push on that waitlist or loop the school counselor in, so it's not just you and that photocopied packet holding this.

*Lets out a long, shuddering breath, wiping my eyes one last time and reaching for my jacket.* 

Yeah. Okay. I appreciate you letting me off the hook with the feelings stuff today. I know that's your job, but if I start unpacking my own baggage right now, I'm never going to make it out to my car. 

I'll definitely take an appointment for next week. And if you actually have some kind of therapist-insider magic trick for getting us bumped up that waitlist, I will absolutely take you up on that. Dealing with the intake coordinators at these clinics is like talking to a brick wall. 

*Stands up, giving a weak but genuine smile.* 

Alright. Write it down, text the wife, do the talk, watch for the red zone. I can do that. Thanks. I'll see you next week. Hopefully with a very boring update about a totally uneventful Tuesday night.
turns.thinking:
I feel a massive wave of relief that she backed off the 'how are you really feeling' stuff. I just can't do it right now. I appreciate that she read the room and let me keep my armor on for the drive home. The summary actually helps. It makes the amorphous, terrifying blob of tonight into a checklist. I can do a checklist. 

And the offer to help with the waitlist? That's the best thing I've heard all month. I'm so tired of fighting the medical bureaucracy by myself. I'm definitely coming back.

judge_analysis:
